subtitle: packed tight, kept apart
body: So far, the line has only been defined, not measured. To see what a Gabor filter does to it, it helps to know that filtering is linear, which means filtering the line as a whole gives the same result as filtering each of its two edges separately and then combining the outputs. So instead of asking what the filter does to the rectangle, we can ask a simpler question about what the filter does to a single step edge.

As already mentioned, the Gabor filter is a windowed oscillating wave packet, and when the filter slides past a single step edge, the result is a ringing and decaying oscillation consisting of a positive lobe, a negative lobe, and a smaller positive lobe...and so on...fading out as the filter moves away from the edge. This reaction is also called the step response.

Each end of the line ($\boldsymbol{\tau_1}$ and $\boldsymbol{\tau_2}$) produces its own step response this way, which corresponds to the dashed and dotted curves in the diagram. Since a line has two edges, filtering it produces two of these distinct step responses and whether these two responses interact depends on their spatial separation and the filter's frequency and angle.
closing: In the first case, the frequency is high, so the oscillations are packed tightly and decay fast. The ripple from $\boldsymbol{\tau_1}$ has completely faded out by the time you get near $\boldsymbol{\tau_2}$, and vice versa. They never overlap, leaving a sum of „ripple, flat, ripple“ meaning the two step responses never interact.
